headline: Anthropic's IPO filing, with $450B of compute commitments, sparked a relief bounce in chips (semis +2.7%), but five-day and one-month infrastructure losses are intact and neoclouds are still the weak link.
regime: Today is a bounce inside a drawdown: the semis ETF rose 2.7% on the day but is still -9.7% on the month and -1.2% over five days, with foundry equipment (-6.8% 5d), grid (-6.9%) and networking/optical (-6.5%) still lagging. The 10-year yield is 4.99% and crude is $101, so the discount rate stays high, though the VIX eased to 17.9. Only ai_software (+8.0% 5d, CRWD +14.8%) is rising over five days, which is rotation rather than build-out confirmation. The Anthropic S-1 is the first hard demand evidence in days, but it also shows how much of that demand rests on outside capital.

theses.title: Power, grid and cooling, not chips, limit the AI build-out
evidence: Grid rose 2.8% on the day but is -6.9% over five days; GE Vernova reports Oct. 28 and Vertiv, which reports Wednesday, closed another acquisition (9d99d2ead3a4, b125cce20890)
Morgan Stanley sees AI power demand going into hyperdrive (84736c150df5)
Pre-revenue nuclear keeps bleeding: Oklo -63% this year, Centrus -33% on the month (265d783304fa, 9661654ca67a)
theses.change_note: Scarcity evidence is steady while prices still reflect financing fear; the earnings of Hubbell, GEV and Vertiv this week are the next test.

theses.title: AI compute demand still outruns supply
evidence: Anthropic's S-1 shows $450B of compute commitments and Broadcom could earn up to $30B from its financing deal (1acee6186fa4, 22878a23f378)
Lumentum says AI components are sold out into 2029; TSMC plans up to 20% higher packaging prices (0dae2c042183, bb2e0ca69775)
Celestica beat on revenue and EPS and cited 2028 customer demand (9e2385d7107e, 656d937947d0)
Against: commitments are only as good as the funding behind them (d74b8df2660c)
theses.change_note: +4: pricing power (TSMC packaging), sold-out optics and a server beat are real supply-tightness signals, not just orders.

theses.title: Debt-funded neoclouds are where the AI cycle breaks first
evidence: CoreWeave, IREN and others hit 52-week lows; CRWV is -52% over six months (cd4f6b62c52b, ea32c2bdbef7)
Musk predicts 'guppy-level death' for the roughly 200 chip renters as SpaceX closes a $40B GPU deal (5bd6ed3323e4)
Segment is -26.0% on the month and -5.7% over five days even as Nebius raised about $280M for France (82e595cac35f)
theses.change_note: -2: Nebius could still raise money and neoclouds bounced on the Anthropic news, but the segment is still at lows and the structural point is unchanged.

theses.title: Memory is priced as if this is the peak of the cycle
evidence: Bank of America sees memory supply tight through the cycle, lifting Seagate and Western Digital (61dc5ba1ac66)
Anthropic's filing lifted MU and SK Hynix (1acee6186fa4)
Segment is still -23.1% on the month, so the multiple has compressed; Seagate reports with raised targets (3d87ee9efd0a)
theses.change_note: +4: a supply-tightness call and a demand anchor arrived while the price is still down about a quarter on the month.

theses.title: Hyperscaler capex is eating their free cash flow
evidence: Meta's $95B AI infrastructure plan weighed on sentiment and Meta is -10.6% over five days; Nvidia is investing $3B in its share offering (889a26ebbebb, 3830a5aa9ebd)
Microsoft is offering buyouts to roughly a quarter of its workforce to pay for AI (20f2e6cb0ce8)
Anthropic and Meta are turning to equity investors for billions (4d57f26ee847)
theses.change_note: Funding is still external, but Nvidia's equity support shows suppliers are propping up customers, a circularity risk rather than relief.

theses.title: The AI trade is crowded and rates are high
evidence: 10-year at 4.99%, crude $101 and the emergency oil reserve at a 1982 low (dfb28bdf56c0)
Semis ETF -9.7% and Nasdaq -2.4% on the month (digest tape)
VIX eased 2.8% on the day to 17.9 and the yield slipped 2.9% over five days, so pressure is easing, not gone
theses.change_note: -4: the VIX and yields eased and the semis bounced; positioning is still stretched but the immediate rate shock softened.

compute.note: +3.2% today but -10.5% on the month; Broadcom upgrades help, funding risk caps it.

foundry_equipment.note: -6.8% over five days (LRCX -12.8%); TSMC's packaging price rise supports the demand side.

memory_storage.note: -23.1% on the month while supply is called tight; Seagate prints now.

networking_optical.note: Lumentum sold out to 2029 but CRDO -12.5% over five days; upgraded from underweight on the demand evidence.

servers.note: Celestica beat and guided up, yet CLS is -17.9% over five days and Dell is under pressure.

power_nuclear.note: Own cash-generating producers; avoid pre-revenue nuclear still bleeding.

grid_electrical.note: -6.9% over five days is financing fear on an intact bottleneck; Hubbell and GE Vernova report.

cooling_thermal.note: Vertiv reports Wednesday; -6.0% over five days with TT the best at -2.1%.

datacenter_neocloud.note: -26.0% on the month and at 52-week lows; avoid until financing clears.

hyperscalers.note: Capex needs outside funding; wait for Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon.

ai_software.note: +8.0% over five days is rotation; CRWD at 189x forward earnings is not a bottleneck play.

risks: Neocloud credit stress could spread to GPU, power and cooling suppliers through cancelled or delayed orders.
A hawkish Fed with the 10-year at 4.99% would extend multiple compression in crowded AI names.
Hyperscaler earnings this week could cut capex guidance and hit the whole supplier chain.
Anthropic's $2 trillion IPO target splits Wall Street; a poor reception would remove the day's support.
Circular financing (Nvidia into Meta, SpaceX into GPUs) can mask weak end demand.
watch: Seagate, Hubbell and Vertiv results for storage, grid and cooling demand.
GE Vernova on Oct. 28 for gas turbine orders.
Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon capex commentary.
Whether the semis bounce holds above today's close with the 10-year under 5%.
Reception of Anthropic's IPO terms and any neocloud debt raises.
